passage_title: The Question I Did Not Ask
student_passage:
The Question I Did Not Ask

For a community-history project, I volunteered to interview Ms. Chen, who had driven city buses for thirty-two years. I arrived with a recorder, two sharpened pencils, and a page of questions about vehicle models and route changes. My finger rested beside the first question as if the paper could conduct the entire conversation for me.[1]

Ms. Chen answered each question politely but briefly. The recorder's red light blinked while the space between us manufactured[2] longer. Then she opened a folder and unfolded a route map covered with penciled stars, none of the stars appeared in the printed legend.[3]

I almost returned to my list. Instead, I asked what the stars meant. Ms. Chen touched each one and explained their[4] purpose: the marks identified stops used by late-shift workers making the final connection home. For example,[5] drivers on two routes sometimes radioed one another when a factory bus was delayed by a few minutes.

There was no official rule requiring the second driver to wait. Ms. Chen described the practice as the most heroic transportation operation in the entire history of civilization.[6] A driver still had to consider the published schedule and other passengers, but a short delay could prevent someone from being stranded after midnight. She remembered one winter evening when she had drove[7] slowly toward the transfer stop until headlights appeared behind her.

A cluster of penciled notes beside one star were[8] faded beyond recognition. [A] Ms. Chen supplied the missing date from memory. [B] I asked her to explain which parts she remembered clearly and which parts she was reconstructing.[9] [C] We recorded both the story and that distinction. [D] After the interview, I photographed the map and linked the image to the audio file.

My prepared questions gave the archive useful dates, route numbers, and equipment details. The penciled stars revealed something those categories had not anticipated: a small practice shaped by judgment, cooperation, and the needs of particular riders. I left the page of questions in the project folder, but I added one at the bottom for my next interview: What in the record still needs to be noticed?[10]
